messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kofi is a 23-year-old Ghanaian-American urban planner who presented for treatment following a severe assault that occurred approximately fourteen months ago. He was attacked late one evening outside a bar by a group of men, at least one of whom had been drinking heavily. The assault began when one of the men threw a glass bottle that struck Kofi on the shoulder, and what followed was a sustained and brutal beating during which he was unable to defend himself or escape. He recalls the smell of alcohol on his attacker's breath as the man leaned over him, and he remembers the sound of shouting — voices distorted by rage — before losing consciousness briefly. When police arrived, they filed a report but made no arrests, and Kofi was left with the understanding that the men who had hurt him would face no consequences. He was discharged from the emergency department the same night with instructions to follow up with his GP, which he did not do.

In the weeks that followed, Kofi found that the memory did not come to him as a continuous narrative. Instead, it arrived in fragments — a frozen image of the bottle leaving the man's hand, a close-up of a face contorted in anger, the specific quality of the pavement against his cheek — each one vivid and complete in itself, but disconnected from the others. When these images surfaced, the emotional weight they carried was so immediate and total that he had to stop whatever he was doing. He could not find words adequate to what had happened; when he tried to tell a friend, what came out felt thin and wrong, and he stopped trying. This inability to organise or articulate the memory meant that it remained unprocessed, and its intrusive return began to feel less like remembering and less like reliving — and the boundary between past and present grew increasingly unreliable. The fragmented nature of the memory also seemed to keep his nervous system perpetually primed, as though the unresolved images signalled to his body that the threat was ongoing.

At work, Kofi spends much of his time in open-plan offices and community consultation meetings, environments where disagreement is routine and voices occasionally rise. He had come to believe that any expression of anger — even a colleague's mild frustration across a conference table — was a signal that violence was imminent. He began arriving early to secure a seat near the exit and would find reasons to leave meetings before they grew contentious. A co-worker's habit of tossing a pen onto the desk when he was thinking could send Kofi's heart into his throat, his body already halfway out of the chair before his mind caught up. The startle responses were relentless: unexpected movement in his peripheral vision, a door closing behind him, someone stepping into his sightline too quickly — each one landed as a genuine threat, and no amount of reassurance from colleagues or friends could convince him otherwise. He was certain, in a way that felt beyond argument, that safety was simply not something that applied to him.

These appraisals — that he was fundamentally unprotected, that institutions had failed him, that he lacked the capacity to cope with ordinary difficulty — fed directly into the strategies he had developed to manage his days. He avoided any situation that might involve conflict, which had begun to limit his professional effectiveness significantly; he had recently declined to lead a community engagement process he had spent months preparing for, telling his supervisor he was unwell. He had also begun gambling online in the evenings, drawn by the way the focused excitement of it temporarily crowded out the images and the dread. But the gambling left him feeling worse about himself the following morning, which deepened his conviction that he was someone who made bad decisions and could not be trusted to manage his own life. This self-blame, rehearsed nightly, kept the negative appraisals vivid and close, which in turn kept his threat system activated — so that the next day he arrived at work already braced, already scanning, and the cycle resumed. The avoidance, paradoxically, had also increased his sensitivity: by never sitting with the discomfort of conflict or anger, he had ensured that each encounter with it felt more dangerous than the last, and the triggers that had once been specific — the smell of alcohol, a thrown object — had broadened.

What finally brought Kofi to seek help was a moment at a neighbourhood planning meeting three weeks ago when a resident raised his voice in frustration and Kofi walked out of the room, sat in his car for forty minutes, and could not return. He told the intake coordinator that he did not expect to feel better, exactly — he was not sure he believed that was possible — but that he could not continue losing pieces of his life to something he could not even properly describe.
